verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them, ‘When a man consecrates a person to Yahweh in a vow, according to your valuation,
your valuation of a male from twenty years old even to sixty years old shall be fifty shekels of silver, after the shekel  of the sanctuary.
If she is a female, then your valuation shall be thirty shekels.
If the person is from five years old even to twenty years old, then your valuation shall be for a male twenty shekels, and for a female ten shekels.
If the person is from a month old even to five years old, then your valuation shall be for a male five shekels of silver, and for a female your valuation shall be three shekels of silver.
If the person is from sixty years old and upward; if he is a male, then your valuation shall be fifteen shekels, and for a female ten shekels.
But if he is poorer than your valuation, then he shall be set before the priest, and the priest shall assign a value to him. The priest shall assign a value according to his ability to pay.
“‘If it is an animal, of which men offer an offering to Yahweh, all that any man gives of such to Yahweh becomes holy.
He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good: and if he shall at all change animal for animal, then both it and that for which it is changed shall be holy.
If it is any unclean animal, of which they do not offer as an offering to Yahweh, then he shall set the animal before the priest;
and the priest shall value it, whether it is good or bad. As you the priest values it, so shall it be.
But if he will indeed redeem it, then he shall add the fifth part of it to its valuation.
“‘When a man dedicates his house to be holy to Yahweh, then the priest shall evaluate it, whether it is good or bad: as the priest shall evaluate it, so shall it stand.
If he who dedicates it will redeem his house, then he shall add the fifth part of the money of your valuation to it, and it shall be his.

“‘If a man dedicates to Yahweh part of the field of his possession, then your valuation shall be according to the seed for it. The sowing of a homer  of barley shall be valued at fifty shekels  of silver.
If he dedicates his field from the Year of Jubilee, according to your valuation it shall stand.

But if he dedicates his field after the Jubilee, then the priest shall reckon to him the money according to the years that remain to the Year of Jubilee; and an abatement shall be made from your valuation.
If he who dedicated the field will indeed redeem it, then he shall add the fifth part of the money of your valuation to it, and it shall remain his.
If he will not redeem the field, or if he has sold the field to another man, it shall not be redeemed any more;
but the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee, shall be holy to Yahweh, as a devoted field. It shall be owned by the priests.
“‘If he dedicates a field to Yahweh which he has bought, which is not of the field of his possession,
then the priest shall reckon to him the worth of your valuation up to the Year of Jubilee; and he shall give your valuation on that day, as a holy thing to Yahweh.
In the Year of Jubilee the field shall return to him from whom it was bought, even to him to whom the possession of the land belongs.
All your valuations shall be according to the shekel of the sanctuary: twenty gerahs  to the shekel.
“‘Only the firstborn among animals, which is made a firstborn to Yahweh, no man may dedicate it; whether an ox or sheep. It is Yahweh’s.

If it is an unclean animal, then he shall buy it back according to your valuation, and shall add to it the fifth part of it; or if it isn’t redeemed, then it shall be sold according to your valuation.

“‘Notwithstanding, no devoted thing, that a man shall devote to Yahweh of all that he has, whether of man or animal, or of the field of his possession, shall be sold or redeemed: every devoted thing is most holy to Yahweh.
“‘No one devoted, who shall be devoted from among men, shall be ransomed; he shall surely be put to death.
“‘All the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is Yahweh’s. It is holy to Yahweh.
If a man redeems anything of his tithe, he shall add a fifth part to it.
All the tithe of the herds or the flocks, whatever passes under the rod, the tenth shall be holy to Yahweh.
He shall not search whether it is good or bad, neither shall he change it. If he changes it at all, then both it and that for which it is changed shall be holy. It shall not be redeemed.’”
These are the commandments which Yahweh commanded Moses for the children of Israel on Mount Sinai.

footnotes.content: The Lord begins with a gentle word to Moses: when you want to give yourself to me, I will tell you how. This closing chapter of Leviticus shows that consecration isn't mystery—it's measured, fair, and within reach for any heart that longs to honor Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A vow to consecrate a person is serious, yet the Lord offers a way to keep it that doesn't break a poor person. He knows our hearts before we speak; He's already thinking of the widow, the struggling widow who wants to give but has little.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fifty shekels for a man in his strength—the prime years, when he carries the weight and the hope of his household. The Lord puts a name to the value, not to diminish any soul, but to set a clear boundary so vows don't bankrupt families.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thirty shekels for a woman—a lower number that speaks to the economics of an ancient household, but notice: she is still valued, still counted, still able to make a vow that the Lord honors. Every voice matters to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Children from five to twenty—the years of learning and growing, when a parent might dedicate a young life to service. The Lord sees their future even when it's unwritten, and His valuation matches what they'll become.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A tiny child, barely remembering words—five shekels for a boy, three for a girl. The Lord doesn't wait for age or understanding; He cherishes the small ones brought to Him in faith, and His measurement is always tender.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At sixty and beyond, the years when strength ebbs but wisdom deepens. Fifteen shekels for an old man, ten for an old woman—the Lord honors the elder still, still counts their prayers, still welcomes their devotion even as the body quiets.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The poorest comes before the priest, and here is mercy written into law: the priest looks not at the scale but at his face, at what he can actually bear. The Lord never meant His altar to be only for the wealthy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When you give an animal to the Lord, it crosses into a different world—holy now, set apart. There's a solemnity in this: what you hand over is no longer yours to treat as before. The Lord takes it seriously; so must you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You cannot swap out a good animal for a weaker one, or a weak one for a strong—no bargaining after the vow. This teaches us something about integrity: when we say 'yes' to the Lord, we don't get to renegotiate when circumstances shift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An unclean animal—one the law says cannot be offered—still has a place before the priest. Even what the law rejects outright, the Lord has a path for. There's always a way for the sincere heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest's eye is careful, judging not in anger but in fairness—good or bad, each animal gets its true worth named. The Lord teaches us through these laws that judgment can be just, and valuation can be humble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If he wishes to take his unclean animal back, he adds a fifth to its price—a price for changing his mind, a small tax on backing out. The Lord builds consequences into grace, so we learn the weight of our choices.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man dedicates his house—not just his livestock, but the very shelter of his family. This is costlier, more personal. The priest evaluates it with care, and what he says stands. The Lord knows this kind of giving cuts deep.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He changes his mind and wants his house back—the Lord allows it, but again, a fifth must be added. There's a pattern: you can undo it, but not without cost. This teaches us that vows aren't chains, yet they aren't cheap.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He dedicates part of his inherited land—a homer of barley brings fifty shekels. Land is memory, livelihood, identity. To give it to the Lord is to say: my future is Yours, my provision is Yours, not my own security.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If the dedication happens in the Jubilee year, the value stands fixed—the great year of release already resets the land's meaning, so the vow stands as spoken. There's an alignment here between God's time and our time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If he dedicates after the Jubilee, the price drops—fewer years before the land reverts anyway. The Lord's law builds in practicality: the closer to Jubilee, the less you give, because the Lord will return it anyway. He doesn't take what He's already going to restore.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If he wants his land back, the fifth is added again—a redemption tax, the same mercy-and-cost pattern. The Lord always gives you a second thought, but He never lets you think cheap thoughts count.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If he neither redeems it nor keeps the gift—if he tries to pass it to another—that choice locks him out. Once a field is wholly given, it's the Lord's forever. There's a point of no return, and the Lord names it clearly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the Jubilee it becomes holy and belongs to the priests—the servants of the altar. The land that was once his now feeds those who feed the people spiritually. One man's devotion becomes another man's provision.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man dedicates land he bought, not inherited—land without family memory or claim. Even a purchased field, stripped of heritage, can be made holy. The Lord receives what we freely choose to give, not only what binds us by blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest counts the years until Jubilee and names a price reflecting that span. The Lord's law is mathematically just: time matters, and what you lose in years shapes what you owe. Nothing escapes His accounting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the Jubilee, the field returns to him from whom it was bought—the original owner, the true possessor. Even if a man gave it away, even if he meant it to be forever gone, the Jubilee restores what was lost. The Lord never lets a sale be truly final.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All valuations follow the sanctuary shekel—the official measure, unchanging, universal. The Lord's measure is not like the world's, which shifts with hunger and greed. His standard holds steady for every person and every gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No one may dedicate the firstborn—it's already the Lord's by the law itself. Some things are not ours to vow, because they already belong to Him. This teaches us wisdom: to recognize what's beyond our power to give.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If it's an unclean animal—a donkey, a camel—he buys it back with a fifth added, or it's sold. The firstborn is the Lord's, but if it cannot be offered, there's still a way to release it. Even in law, the Lord leaves room to breathe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A devoted thing—fully devoted—can never be redeemed or sold; it remains most holy. This is the highest vow, the ultimate gift: no backing out, no buyback, only holiness. Some surrenders are meant to be forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A person devoted to the Lord cannot be ransomed—an ancient rule reflecting the gravity of a life wholly given. Whether this speaks of temple service or a deeper consequence, the point stands: total devotion has no middle ground.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the tithe belongs to the Lord—a tenth of seed and fruit, set aside before anything else is claimed. The farmer looks at his harvest and says: You first. This is the rhythm of gratitude, written into the soil itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If he redeems his tithe—takes it back in silver—a fifth is added to its worth. Even the tenth, which is already the Lord's, costs something to reclaim. The Lord doesn't begrudge us, but He never lets us imagine provision is free.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The tithe of herds or flocks: every tenth animal that passes under the rod belongs to the Lord. No picking the strongest, no choosing favorites—the rod chooses, and the Lord takes what comes. He wants what you cannot control, so you learn to trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't search or judge whether it's good or bad—don't look to save a weak one. Accept the tenth that falls; both it and any swap are equally holy. The Lord asks for surrender, not strategy; for trust, not cleverness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this final verse: these laws, given at Sinai so long ago, still teach us that the Lord is generous—He takes our gifts seriously, offers buyback grace, and never forgets the poor. As of 2026-10, His care hasn't changed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
